lessons.title: Timeouts and after-timeout plays
lessons.objective: Explain why coaches call timeouts and what an ATO is.

payload.prompt: Why do coaches call timeouts?

options.text: To rest players, talk strategy, stop opponent momentum, or set up a play.
To avoid taking a technical foul.
To adjust the scoreboard.

explanation.correct: A timeout stops the clock so a coach can rest players, change the plan, cool off an opponent's run or draw up a play. Each team has a limited number, so when to use them is part of the strategy.
explanation.incorrect: Timeouts are a coaching tool, not a penalty fix or a scoreboard change. They give a team a moment to rest, regroup and set up the next few possessions.

payload.prompt: What is an after-timeout play (ATO)?

options.text: A play the coach draws up in a timeout and runs when play resumes.
Any play run after the ball goes out of bounds.
A play where every player takes a turn shooting.

explanation.correct: An ATO is designed during a timeout for a specific situation, like getting a good shot late in a game. The defense has had the same time to prepare, which is part of the chess match.
explanation.incorrect: An after-timeout play is not any out-of-bounds play. It is a set the coach draws up in the huddle and runs as soon as play restarts.

payload.prompt: Complete the definition of a run.
payload.template: A run is a string of {{points}} points by one team, often ended when the other coach calls a {{stop}}.

explanation.correct: A run is points scored in a row while the other team does not score, like a 12-0 burst. The coach on the wrong end often calls a timeout to stop it.
explanation.incorrect: A run needs unanswered points, meaning the other team has not scored in between. A timeout is the usual way a coach tries to stop one.

payload.prompt: The lead is shrinking fast. Call a timeout?

situation.narrative: Your team led by 15. The other team just went on a 12-0 run, the lead is 3, and they have the ball again with the crowd roaring.

options.label: Call a timeout
options.consequence: You stop the run, settle your players and change something, like a coverage or the lineup. You still have timeouts left for the end of the game.
considerations: A 12-0 run shows something is broken
You still have two timeouts for late in the game
It also rests tired starters

options.label: Wait one more possession
options.consequence: You hope the next stop comes on its own. If they score again, the lead is nearly gone and the crowd is deafening.
considerations: The run has already cost 12 points
Timeouts are there to be used
Waiting only makes sense if the defense just fixed itself

payload.expertNote: Coaches call a timeout when a run exposes a real problem, not after every basket. The value is changing something, not just pausing. Saving timeouts for the last minutes matters, but holding all three while a 15-point lead melts is not a strategy.

payload.question: What is she talking about?

options.text: The coach drew up a great set play during the timeout that resulted in a score.
The team scored right after taking a break.
A player made a timeout-related error.
The team's time management was bad.

payload.translation: She means the play the coach drew up in the timeout worked perfectly and got a good shot.

followUps.why: It is an honest question that lets her describe the play, and you pick up the vocabulary from her.

followUps.line: Who did he call the play for?
followUps.why: A natural follow-up asking which player the play was designed to get open.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: An ATO is just a play drawn up in a timeout. If you did not catch the details, asking which player it was for is a perfectly good question.

lessons.title: Rotations and minutes
lessons.objective: Follow starters, bench units and staggered stars.

payload.prompt: What is the starting five?

options.text: The five players who begin the game for a team.
The five players with the most fouls.
Five substitutes waiting on the bench.

explanation.correct: The starting five are the lineup on the floor at tip-off. They are usually a team's most important players, though a coach may start a role player for the matchup and bring a star off the bench.
explanation.incorrect: The starting five are simply the five who begin the game. Players who sit on the bench are the reserves, and fouls have nothing to do with it.

payload.prompt: Complete the definition of a team's rotation.
payload.template: A team's rotation is the group of players a coach {{who}}, and how many {{what}} each one gets.

explanation.correct: A rotation is the set of players who get real playing time and the minutes each one plays. A coach with nine players in the rotation uses more of the roster than one who uses seven.
explanation.incorrect: A rotation is about who plays and for how long, not who was drafted or how many fouls they have. Its size shapes how the team looks in close games.

payload.prompt: What is a bench unit?

options.text: A group of reserves who usually play together as a second lineup.
The bench where substitutes sit.
The starters who rest during a timeout.

explanation.correct: A bench unit is the second-team lineup that checks in together. Coaches build it to hold the lead, or cut into a deficit, while the starters rest.
explanation.incorrect: The furniture is not the unit, and resting starters are still starters. A bench unit is the set of reserves who play together as a lineup.

payload.prompt: Fill in the blanks about staggering stars.
payload.template: When a coach staggers minutes, the stars sit at {{gap-1}} times, so at least one star is {{gap-2}}.

explanation.correct: Staggering means the stars rest at different times. One star is always in the game to lead the offense, so the team does not fall apart while the others sit.
explanation.incorrect: If all the stars sat together the team would sink, and if they all played at once nobody would rest. Staggering spreads the rest so a star is on the floor at all times.

payload.question: What is she saying about the team?

options.text: The coach plays only a handful of players, and they play a lot.
Most of the players on the team are short.
The quarters are shorter than normal.
The team keeps making quick substitutions.

payload.translation: She means the coach relies on a small core group and gives them heavy minutes instead of spreading playing time over many players.

followUps.line: How many guys are actually playing?
followUps.why: It is an easy question, and her answer tells you how short is short.

followUps.line: Does that hurt them if somebody gets hurt?
followUps.why: A short rotation leaves little depth, so injuries and fatigue matter more. It is a good thing to wonder about.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: A short rotation just means a few players carry the load. If you want a number, ask her how many players get real minutes.

lessons.title: Small ball and matchups
lessons.objective: Explain small ball, two-big lineups and switchability.

payload.prompt: What is small ball?

options.text: Smaller, quicker players instead of traditional big men, prioritizing perimeter shooting and pace.
Playing with a smaller basketball.
Reducing the game time for each player.

explanation.correct: Right. Small ball is a lineup with faster, shootier players and few or no traditional centers.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. Small ball is using smaller, more perimeter-oriented players to spread the floor and play faster.

payload.prompt: What is a two-big lineup used for?

options.text: Gaining rebounding and rim protection, in exchange for some floor spacing.
Running more fast breaks with two speedy guards.
Getting more three-point shooters on the floor.

explanation.correct: Two bigs protect the rim and crash the boards, but they usually stand closer to the basket, which can crowd the lane. Coaches use them when the matchup favors size.
explanation.incorrect: A two-big lineup is the opposite of a speedy, shooting lineup. It buys size, rebounding and rim protection, and pays for it with floor spacing.

payload.prompt: What does switchability mean in defense?

options.text: Being able to guard different positions well, so a switch costs nothing.
Changing the defense every quarter.
Being quick to swap jerseys at halftime.

explanation.correct: Switchable players can guard a guard, a wing or a big for a few possessions. A team full of them can switch every screen without giving up a mismatch.
explanation.incorrect: Switchability has nothing to do with halves or jerseys. It describes players who can defend several positions, which is what makes switching screens safe.

payload.prompt: Match their small lineup or stay big?

situation.narrative: Your team is down 5 with six minutes left. The other team went small and its shooters have made four threes in four minutes. Your center is a good rebounder but struggles to guard in space.

facts.label: Their lineup
facts.value: Small, four shooters, four threes made

facts.label: Your center
facts.value: Good rebounder, slow defending in space

options.label: Go small to match
options.consequence: A quicker lineup can stay with their shooters and switch screens, though you give up some size on the boards.
considerations: Your center is the weak link against their shooting
A switchable lineup closes out on threes
You will be smaller, so rebounding gets harder

options.label: Keep your center in
options.consequence: You keep your rebounding and rim protection, but your center is stuck defending in space against shooters.
considerations: Their misses are harder to rebound against your size
The center may get picked on in pick-and-rolls
It is a reasonable bet if he can drop and contest

payload.expertNote: Coaches weigh what each lineup gives and takes. Small ball buys speed and spacing and costs size. Here the opponent's shooting is the problem, so matching is sensible, but a coach who trusts his center in drop coverage could stay big.

payload.prompt: Hunt the mismatch or play it straight?

situation.narrative: After a switch, their 6'3" wing shooter is now guarding your 7-foot center. The other team may switch back soon.

facts.label: Mismatch
facts.value: Big size advantage in the post

options.label: Hunt the mismatch: feed the post
options.consequence: Your big can score over the smaller defender or draw help and pass out. If they double, a shooter is left open.
considerations: The height gap is big, so the post is easy to exploit
Their shooter may pick up fouls guarding a big
They may switch back or send help, so act quickly

options.label: Run your normal offense
options.consequence: You let the defense fix the matchup, and a clear advantage goes unused.
considerations: The switch handed you a size edge
A quick feed to the post uses it before they switch back
Normal offense is fine when there is no edge

payload.expertNote: Offenses go right at a mismatch before the defense can fix it. The catch is the help: if the post gets crowded, the big has to be able to pass back out.

payload.question: What does she mean?

options.text: A lineup of quick shooters is giving the other team's defense trouble.
The other team has very short players.
The other team keeps running out of bounds.
The other team needs to use a smaller ball.

payload.translation: A team is playing quick, shooting players instead of bigs, and the opponent's defense cannot keep up with the spacing and speed.

followUps.line: Is it their bigs that can't keep up?
followUps.why: It shows you understand small ball stretches big defenders, and it gets her talking about the matchup.
A fair question about how coaches respond to each other's lineups.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Small ball is just quicker, smaller players who can shoot instead of big men. If she says it about a team, you can ask who is playing center.

lessons.title: Foul or not: end-of-game math
lessons.objective: Decide when to foul, when to defend and why up-3 is tricky.

payload.prompt: Up three with six seconds left. Foul or defend?

situation.narrative: Your team leads by 3. The other team has the ball with six seconds left and needs a three to tie. They are in the bonus, so a foul sends them to the line.

options.label: Foul before they can shoot
options.consequence: They get two free throws. To tie they must make the first, miss the second on purpose and win the rebound, so a three cannot tie on the spot. But a badly timed foul can send a shooter to the line for three.
considerations: It takes away the tying three
They could still tie with a planned miss and a putback
A foul on a three-point shooter gives them three shots

options.label: Defend the three
options.consequence: They have to get a clean look from deep against a defense that knows what is coming. If it goes in, the game goes to overtime.
considerations: Covering the arc is hard in six seconds
A made three forces overtime
It avoids the risk of fouling a shooter

payload.expertNote: There is no single right answer. Analysts have argued that fouling is slightly better on average, but many coaches still defend, because a bad foul or an offensive rebound on a missed free throw costs them the game. Fans argue about it every season.

payload.prompt: Down four with twelve seconds left. Foul?

situation.narrative: Your team trails by 4 with twelve seconds left. The other team has the ball in the frontcourt and is in the bonus. If you just defend, they can hold the ball until time runs out.

facts.label: Their status
facts.value: In the bonus, ball in the frontcourt

facts.label: If you do nothing
facts.value: They can dribble out the clock

options.label: Foul right away
options.consequence: The clock stops and they shoot two free throws. You are likely still trailing, but you keep a chance at one more possession, which is better than certain defeat.
considerations: Without a foul the clock keeps running for them
Each free throw they miss gives you the ball
The cost is that they may score more points

options.label: Defend and hope for a turnover
options.consequence: They can burn the clock with no risk. By the time they shoot, your team has almost no chance to catch up.
considerations: Turnovers are rare when the other team just holds the ball
You give up your clock-stopping tool
Down four with twelve seconds, time is the problem

payload.expertNote: The trailing team fouls to stop the clock, and the price is free-throw points. It is worth it only when time is about to win the game for them. Poor free-throw shooters are the best targets, which is what the next lesson's hack-a-player idea is about.

payload.prompt: Hack a 55% free-throw shooter early in the half?

situation.narrative: Midway through the third quarter, the other team's big man is a 55% free-throw shooter. Your coach wonders whether to foul him on purpose every time he gets the ball.

facts.label: Quarter
facts.value: Third, with plenty of time left

facts.label: Rule
facts.value: Away-from-the-play fouls are penalized in the last two minutes of a quarter

options.label: Hack him when he has the ball
options.consequence: He scores about 1.1 points per trip, which is less than a normal offensive possession, but your own offense gets no stops or rhythm and you pile up fouls.
considerations: 1.1 points is below a typical possession
It breaks the game up, which can hurt your own flow
You will hit the penalty quickly and give others free throws

options.label: Defend him normally
options.consequence: He scores at the normal rate near the basket, but your team stays in rhythm and avoids foul trouble.
considerations: Your defense can still contest his shots
It does not hand out free points
It does not use his weakness

payload.expertNote: Hack-a-player is a real strategy and a real argument. The math favors it only when a player is truly bad from the line and the offense is otherwise efficient, and the league's away-from-the-play rule for the end of quarters limits it. Many coaches decide it is not worth the disruption.

payload.prompt: Why do teams often hold the ball for the last shot?

options.text: So the other team has too little time left to answer.
Because the shot clock is turned off at the end of games.
Because the league requires the trailing team to shoot last.

explanation.correct: In a tie game, the team that shoots last can leave the other team no time to respond. It runs the clock down and then runs a play for its best option, often after a timeout.
explanation.incorrect: The shot clock is on at the end of games and no rule assigns the last shot. Teams hold the ball to use the clock, so the other team cannot answer.

payload.prompt: Why do coaches give intentional fouls late in games?

options.text: To reset possession, adjust the shot clock or stop the clock in specific late-game scenarios.
To make the opponent angry.
To teach players a lesson.

explanation.correct: Exactly. Strategic fouls are about time management and possession, not emotion.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. Intentional fouls are tactical: they reset the clock or give your team back the ball in tight moments.

payload.question: What is she talking about?

options.text: The opponent is deliberately fouling a poor free-throw shooter to send him to the line instead of letting him play.
A player is coughing (hacking)..
They are using a computer exploit in the game.
A player's defense is very sloppy.

payload.translation: She means the opponent is intentionally fouling a bad FT shooter to try to disrupt them and their rhythm.

followUps.line: Yeah, he's missing everything from the line.
followUps.why: You see that the hack strategy is working; the shooter is struggling at the free-throw line.

followUps.line: At what point do they stop doing it?
followUps.why: A good follow-up asking whether there's a point in the game where hacking becomes less effective.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Hacking is just fouling a bad FT shooter on purpose to send them to the line instead of letting them play.

lessons.title: Two-for-one and clock management
lessons.objective: Calculate when to shoot early to get two possessions.

payload.prompt: Tap to shoot for two possessions before the half ends.

explanation.correct: Right! You shot with enough time (around 30+ seconds) left so your opponent shoots, and you get the ball back before the half ends.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. Two-for-one means you shoot while there is enough time (usually 30+ seconds) left so both teams get one more possession each.

payload.prompt: Tap when you should call timeout to stop the clock.

explanation.correct: Nice! You stopped the clock at a key moment, giving your team time to set up the play you need.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. Timeout timing is about stopping the clock when you need it most—usually with enough time to set a play.

payload.prompt: With how many seconds left can you still get two possessions?

explanation.correct: Right around there. 30 seconds is the typical threshold: you have time to shoot, they have time to shoot, and you get the ball back.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. Roughly 30 seconds is the benchmark. Any more and you could afford a longer possession; any less and they might not get a real shot.

payload.prompt: How many timeouts does an NBA team get per quarter?

explanation.correct: Right. Three timeouts per quarter (with one carryover if unused). That is why coaches use them carefully.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. NBA teams get three timeouts per quarter, with one unused timeout carrying over to the next quarter.

payload.prompt: How should you run the final possession?

situation.narrative: Your team is down 2 with 8 seconds left. You have the ball. No timeouts remain. Your best scorer is being double-teamed.

options.label: ISO your best scorer
options.consequence: They are double-teamed and have to create. Risky but your star might force a shot or find an open teammate.
considerations: Star scorers sometimes break double-teams
But only 8 seconds is very tight
No timeout means no reset if they don't get off a shot

options.label: Quick ball movement
options.consequence: You move the ball fast to find the open man from the double. No timeout = simplicity and speed.
considerations: Doubles create gaps; find them quickly
8 seconds is not much time for a complex play
Quick movement often beats heroics late

payload.expertNote: Final possession with no timeouts? Move the ball fast. Doubles create openings. Your best shot is the next guy over, not forcing it through two defenders.

lessons.title: Series chess: adjustments
lessons.objective: Understand how coaches adjust from game to game in a playoff series.

payload.prompt: What is a series adjustment?

options.text: Changes a coach makes from game to game based on what worked and what did not in the series.
A change to the schedule of playoff games.
Adjusting the rules for playoff basketball.

explanation.correct: Right. Coaches adjust their strategy, lineups and plays between games based on what they learn.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. Series adjustments are strategic changes coaches make after each game based on outcomes and opponent patterns.

payload.prompt: Why do coaches shrink their rotation in the playoffs?

options.text: To give more minutes to their best players and bench depth is less important when every game is critical.
To rest everyone equally.
Because there are fewer games in the playoffs.

explanation.correct: Exactly. Playoffs reward your elite players. Coaches use fewer people and trust their stars more.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. Playoff rotations shrink because coaches want their best five or six players on the floor as much as possible.

payload.prompt: What is home-court advantage worth?

options.text: A few points on average due to fan support, travel rest and familiarity with the court.
An automatic win in the series.
Extra timeouts at home.

explanation.correct: Right. Home court gives you 2-3 points of edge on average from noise, rest and comfort.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. Home-court advantage is worth a few points per game on average from fan noise and travel rest.

payload.prompt: How should you adjust after Game 1?

situation.narrative: You lost Game 1 of a playoff series at home, 102-95. Opponent's 7-footer dominated the post, scoring 24. Your small-ball lineup gave up offensive rebounds.

facts.label: Your edge
facts.value: You have a strong perimeter game

options.label: Go with two-big lineups for Game 2
options.consequence: You address the post and rebound problem. You lose some spacing but control the paint better.
considerations: The 7-footer hurt you; address it directly
Rebounding margin matters in a series
Sacrifice some spacing to protect the basket

options.label: Stay with small ball
options.consequence: You get torched in the post again and give up the rebounding battle.
considerations: Same problem, same result
Adjustments mean changing what did not work
Ignoring the 7-footer is a loss

payload.expertNote: Post got destroyed in Game 1? Go bigger in Game 2. Sacrificing spacing to shut down a post threat is a smart series move.

statement.speaker: Your crush
statement.text: Coach made a good adjustment for Game 2.

payload.question: What is she talking about?

options.text: The coach changed the strategy or lineup after Game 1, addressing a problem that hurt them.
The referee made a better call in Game 2.
The coach sat down during the game.
They won Game 2.

payload.translation: She's saying the coach smartly changed something (a play, a lineup, a coverage) after learning from Game 1, and it worked better.

followUps.line: Yeah, they finally covered the post.
followUps.why: You recognize that the adjustment specifically targeted a weakness from the previous game.
A good follow-up about the ongoing strategic back-and-forth in a series.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Adjustments are just coaches changing what did not work. If the post was a problem, go bigger. If perimeter was a problem, go smaller.

lessons.title: Load management and back-to-backs
lessons.objective: Explain rest, back-to-backs and the 65-game rule.

payload.prompt: What is load management?

options.text: Strategic rest for healthy stars to prevent injury and keep them fresh for playoffs.
Making sure a player can carry the ball to the locker room.
Limiting how heavy a player's dribble is.

explanation.correct: Right. Load management is sitting out healthy players to rest them during the regular season.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. Load management is strategic rest given to stars during the season to reduce wear and tear.

payload.prompt: What is a back-to-back?

options.text: Two games played on consecutive nights, which is tiring and affects player rest.
When two players defend each other.
When a player scores twice in a row.

explanation.correct: Exactly. Back-to-backs are two games in a row, and fatigue can be a factor in the second game.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. A back-to-back is simply playing on consecutive nights, which wears on players and teams.

payload.prompt: What is the 65-game rule in the NBA?

options.text: A team should play at least 65 games per season; star players sitting out more loses draft position and playoff seeding.
A game ends after 65 points are scored.
Teams must practice for 65 minutes a day.

explanation.correct: Right. The 65-game threshold is a soft standard that discourages load management; teams that play most games stay in title contention.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. The 65-game guideline is an NBA soft rule: play your stars enough or you lose playoff seeding or draft position.

payload.prompt: Fill in the blanks about load management.
payload.template: Load management means a coach {{gap-1}} a healthy star player to {{gap-2}} them for the playoffs, even though it costs regular-season wins.

explanation.correct: Right. Load management is a strategy to protect stars from overuse during the regular season.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. Load management is coaches strategically resting healthy players to preserve them for the playoffs.

statement.speaker: Your crush
statement.text: He is out tonight for load management.

payload.question: What does she mean?

options.text: The coach is resting a healthy player to keep him fresh and reduce injury risk during the regular season.
The player is injured and out for the season.
The player is carrying too many bags.
The player is managing the team's finances.

payload.translation: She means the coach is benching a star player on purpose, even though he is healthy, to rest him for the playoffs.

followUps.why: You recognize that back-to-backs are a common reason for load management.

followUps.line: How many games has he missed?
followUps.why: A good follow-up tracking how many games a player has been rested this season.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Load management is just resting a healthy star to keep him fresh. The team wins less games but the star is ready for playoffs.

statement.speaker: Your crush
statement.text: That team looks tired; it is their fourth game in five nights.

payload.question: What is she noticing?

options.text: The team is fatigued from playing many games in a short span, including back-to-backs, which affects performance.
The team played four consecutive 5-minute games.
The team has played five seasons in four years.
The players are literally tired and need to sleep.

payload.translation: She's saying the schedule is brutal—multiple games close together—and you can see the fatigue in how the team is playing.

followUps.line: Yeah, they got smoked in the third quarter.
followUps.why: You recognize that tired teams lose energy late in games, especially over a busy stretch.

followUps.line: Do they have any rest days coming up?
followUps.why: A good follow-up asking when the team can recover in the schedule.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Back-to-backs and road trips wear on teams. Three or four games in five nights? Fatigue is real.
